questions.title: What is blockchain?
questions.text: Describe what blockchain technology is.

scheme.mark_scheme: A distributed database shared among the nodes of a network / a growing list of records (blocks) linked using cryptography / a technology for a secure, decentralised record of transactions (1). Accept any reasonable description.
scheme.model_answer: A decentralised, distributed ledger: a growing list of blocks of transactions linked by hashes and copied to every node of the network.

questions.title: Uses
questions.text: Give **one** example of using blockchain technology.

scheme.mark_scheme: Cryptocurrencies / Bitcoin / Ethereum; smart contracts; financial services; games / NFTs; supply chain; domain names; certificates; voting (1)
scheme.model_answer: Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin.

questions.title: Key terms
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

A blockchain is a distributed [[1]] of transactions. Each computer that keeps a copy of it is called a [[2]]. Every block stores the [[3]] of the previous block. The first block of the chain is called the [[4]] block.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) ledger / database (2) node (3) hash (4) genesis

questions.title: Contents of a block
questions.text: Which **three** of these are stored in a block of a blockchain?

scheme.mark_scheme: A, C, E

options.content: The hash of the previous block
The private keys of the users
The password of the central administrator

questions.title: Blockchain vocabulary
questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: Fixed-length fingerprint calculated from the data
Number changed by miners to find a valid hash
Computer that keeps a copy of the ledger
Program on the blockchain that runs automatically when conditions are met

questions.title: Hash properties
questions.text: A SHA-256 hash can be decrypted to get back the original block data.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Hashing is one-way; it is not encryption.

questions.title: Avalanche effect
questions.text:
`Aida pays Bek 10` has the SHA-256 hash `58fac423…1e726b74`, but `Aida pays Bek 90` has the hash `b5ac3f09…4086512a`.

Explain what this shows about hash functions and why it is useful in a blockchain.

scheme.mark_scheme: A tiny change in the data gives a completely different hash / avalanche effect (1); so any change to a block's data is detected immediately because the stored hash no longer matches (1)
scheme.model_answer: Changing one digit produces a totally different hash. So if anyone alters a block, its hash changes and the change is detected at once.

questions.title: Linking blocks
questions.text: Explain how the blocks of a blockchain are linked together.

scheme.mark_scheme: Each block contains the hash of the previous block (1); so the blocks form a chain in order back to the genesis block / a change breaks the link (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every block stores the hash of the block before it, which links the blocks in order back to the genesis block.

questions.title: Tamper resistance
questions.text: Explain why it is very difficult to change a transaction that is already recorded in a blockchain.

scheme.mark_scheme: Changing the data changes the block's hash (1); the next block's 'previous hash' no longer matches, so the chain is broken / all later blocks would need re-mining (1); every node has a copy and the majority version is accepted, so the altered copy is rejected (1)
scheme.model_answer: The block's hash would change, so it would no longer match the previous-hash stored in the next block; the attacker would have to re-mine every later block, and the other nodes' copies would still show the original, so the change would be rejected.

questions.title: Adding a transaction
questions.text: Put the stages of adding a transaction in order by writing 1–5 in the second column.

prefill: Nodes validate the signature and the balance
The user signs the transaction with a private key
The block is added to every copy of the chain
The transaction is broadcast to the network
Nodes reach consensus, e.g. proof of work

questions.title: Keys
questions.text: State what each key is used for in a blockchain transaction.

scheme.mark_scheme: Private key: kept secret, used to sign the transaction (1); public key: shared, used by others / nodes to verify the signature (or as the address to receive coins) (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Private key: kept secret and used to sign the transaction.
Public key: shared so that nodes can verify the signature.

questions.title: Mining
questions.text: Describe the role of miners in a proof-of-work blockchain.

scheme.mark_scheme: Validate transactions and group them into a block (1); compete to solve the puzzle — change the nonce until the hash meets the target — and the winner adds the block and is rewarded (1)
scheme.model_answer: Miners check transactions and put them into a block, then repeatedly change the nonce until the block's hash meets the difficulty target; the first to succeed adds the block and earns a reward.

questions.title: Proof of work or stake?
questions.text: Tick (✓) the consensus mechanism each statement describes.

prefill: Uses a very large amount of electricity
Validators lock up their own coins
Miners change a nonce to find a valid hash
A cheating validator can lose its coins

scheme.mark_scheme: PoW; PoS; PoW; PoS (1 each)

questions.title: Central vs distributed
questions.text: Which statement describes a blockchain but **not** a central bank database?

scheme.mark_scheme: B

options.content: Every node keeps a full copy of the records
Transactions have a date and time

questions.title: Smart contracts
questions.text: Describe a smart contract and give an example of its use.

scheme.mark_scheme: A program stored on the blockchain that runs automatically when conditions are met (1); example, e.g. payment released when delivery is confirmed / insurance paid when a flight is delayed (1)
scheme.model_answer: A program on the blockchain that executes automatically when agreed conditions are met, e.g. paying a supplier as soon as delivery is confirmed.

questions.title: 51 % attack
questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 51 % attack and why it is unlikely on a large public blockchain.

scheme.mark_scheme: A group controls more than half of the computing power / stake and can rewrite recent blocks / approve its own version (1); on a large network this needs an enormous amount of hardware and electricity, so it is too expensive (1)
scheme.model_answer: If one group controlled over half the network's computing power it could out-mine the honest nodes and rewrite recent blocks; on a network like Bitcoin this would cost far too much.

questions.title: Types of blockchain
questions.text: Match each type of blockchain to its description.

right.text: Anyone can read, send transactions and run a node
Only invited members of one organisation
Controlled by a group of organisations

questions.title: Advantages and disadvantages
questions.text: State **two** advantages and **two** disadvantages of blockchain technology.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantages (1 each, max 2): hard to tamper / data integrity; no central authority / no single point of failure; transparent; fewer intermediaries / lower fees; permanent audit trail. Disadvantages (1 each, max 2): high energy use (PoW); slow; mistakes cannot be undone / lost keys; large storage; legal uncertainty; privacy on public chains.
scheme.model_answer:
Advantage 1: records are very hard to tamper with.
Advantage 2: no single point of failure.
Disadvantage 1: proof of work uses a lot of electricity.
Disadvantage 2: lost private keys mean lost assets.

questions.title: Tracking medicines
questions.text: A pharmaceutical company uses blockchain to record every step of a medicine's journey from the factory to the pharmacy.

scheme.mark_scheme: Distributed database shared among nodes / list of blocks linked using cryptography / secure decentralised record of transactions (1)
scheme.model_answer: A decentralised ledger of records grouped into blocks linked by hashes and copied to many nodes.

parts.title: Block contents
parts.text: State **three** items stored in each block.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): data / transactions (e.g. location of the medicine); timestamp; hash of the block; hash of the previous block; nonce; block number
scheme.model_answer:
1 The data, e.g. where the batch was delivered
2 A timestamp
3 The hash of the previous block

parts.title: Fake records
parts.text: A criminal wants to change an old record to hide a batch of fake medicines. Explain why this would be detected.

scheme.mark_scheme: Changing the record changes the block's hash (1); it no longer matches the previous hash stored in the next block / every later block would have to be recalculated (1); other nodes hold the original copy, so the majority rejects the change (1)
scheme.model_answer: The edited block would get a new hash that does not match the next block's previous-hash, so the chain breaks; all the other nodes still hold the original chain, so the altered copy is rejected.

parts.title: Other use
parts.text: Give **one** other example of using blockchain technology.

scheme.mark_scheme: Cryptocurrency; smart contracts; financial services; games; domain names; certificates; voting; land registry (1)
scheme.model_answer: Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin.

questions.title: Cryptocurrency payments
questions.text: Dana sends 0.5 coins of a cryptocurrency to Arman.

parts.title: Process
parts.text: Describe how Dana's transaction is added to the blockchain.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): Dana signs the transaction with her private key; it is broadcast to the network of nodes; nodes validate it (signature / enough balance); it is grouped with others into a block; nodes reach consensus / a miner solves the proof of work; the block is added to every copy of the chain
scheme.model_answer: Dana signs the transaction with her private key and it is broadcast to the nodes. The nodes validate the signature and her balance, then put it in a block with other transactions. A miner solves the proof of work and the block is added to every copy of the chain.

parts.title: Keys
parts.text: Explain the purpose of Dana's private key and public key.

scheme.mark_scheme: Private: secret, used to sign / authorise the transaction, proving it is from Dana (1); public: shared, used by nodes to verify the signature / as her address (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Private key: kept secret; Dana signs the transaction with it.
Public key: nodes use it to check that the signature is Dana's.

parts.title: Compare
parts.text: Compare recording this payment on a blockchain with recording it in a bank's central database.

scheme.mark_scheme: Blockchain: copied to many nodes / decentralised, no single owner (1); bank: one organisation controls and can edit the records / single point of failure / users must trust the bank (1)
scheme.model_answer: On a blockchain every node has a copy and no one controls it, while a bank's database is held and controlled by one organisation that users must trust.

questions.title: Consensus and certificates
questions.text: Nodes of a blockchain must agree before a new block is added.

parts.title: Proof of work
parts.text: Explain how proof of work is used to add a new block.

scheme.mark_scheme: Miners compete to solve a puzzle (1); repeatedly change the nonce and calculate the hash until it meets the target, e.g. starts with zeros (1); the first miner broadcasts the block, others check it easily and add it; the miner is rewarded (1)
scheme.model_answer: Miners compete: each changes the nonce and recalculates the block's hash until it starts with the required zeros. The first to succeed broadcasts the block; other nodes quickly verify it and add it, and the miner gets a reward.

parts.title: Proof of stake
parts.text: State **one** disadvantage of proof of work and explain how proof of stake reduces it.

scheme.mark_scheme: PoW uses huge amounts of electricity (1); PoS chooses validators by the coins they stake, so no energy-intensive puzzle is needed (1)
scheme.model_answer: Proof of work uses a lot of electricity; proof of stake picks validators by their staked coins, so no puzzle has to be solved.

parts.title: Hash
parts.text: State **one** property of a cryptographic hash function.

scheme.mark_scheme: Fixed length / deterministic / one-way / small change gives a completely different hash / collision-resistant (1)
scheme.model_answer: A small change in the data gives a completely different hash.

parts.title: Certificates
parts.text: A university plans to store its diplomas on a blockchain. Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of this plan.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage: employers can verify diplomas / they cannot be forged or changed (1); disadvantage: mistakes cannot be easily corrected / personal data visible / cost, energy, storage / lost keys (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Advantage: employers can check a diploma is genuine because it cannot be forged.
Disadvantage: a wrong record cannot simply be edited or deleted.

summary: What blockchain technology is — a decentralised, distributed ledger compared with a central database; its key properties; the structure of a block (data, timestamp, nonce, hash, previous hash) and the genesis block; hash functions and the avalanche effect; public and private keys, digital signatures and wallets; how a transaction is added; consensus — proof of work, mining and proof of stake; why the chain is tamper-resistant and the 51 % attack; public, private and consortium blockchains; smart contracts and other uses; advantages and disadvantages.

blocks.content: A **decentralised, distributed digital ledger** (a shared database) in which records — usually **transactions** — are grouped into **blocks** that are **linked together using cryptography** (hashes). A copy of the whole chain is kept on many computers (**nodes**), so the records cannot be changed without everyone noticing.
A **record of transactions** — who sent what to whom and when. A bank keeps a ledger of all its customers' payments.

blocks.title: Central database or blockchain?
rows: **Copied** to every node in a **peer-to-peer** network
The owner can **edit or delete** records
Records are **append-only** — new blocks are added, old ones are not changed
Trust comes from **cryptography** and **consensus** of the nodes
A **single point of failure** — if the server is attacked, data may be lost
No single point of failure — other nodes still have copies
Often **transparent** — anyone can check the records

blocks.content:
CENTRALISED                         DISTRIBUTED (BLOCKCHAIN)

   User   User   User                   Node ────── Node ────── Node
     \     |     /                     [copy]      [copy]      [copy]
      \    |    /                        │    \      │      /    │
     ┌─────────────┐                     │     \     │     /     │
     │ Bank server │                   Node ────── Node ────── Node
     │  (ledger)   │                  [copy]      [copy]      [copy]
     └─────────────┘
   One owner, one copy               Every node keeps the whole ledger
blocks.caption: Centralised and distributed ledgers

items.title: Decentralised
items.content: No central authority (bank, government) controls it; decisions are made by the network.

items.title: Distributed
items.content: Every **node** stores a **full copy** of the ledger and the copies are kept in sync.

items.title: Immutable
items.content: Once a block is added it is practically **impossible to change** — data has high **integrity**.

items.title: Transparent
items.content: On a public blockchain anyone can **view and verify** all transactions (users appear only as addresses).

items.title: Consensus-based
items.content: Nodes must **agree** that a new block is valid before it is added.

blocks.title: What a block contains
rows: Position of the block in the chain
The transactions (sender, receiver, amount) or other records
The hash of the block **before** it — this is what **links** the chain
A number changed by miners to find a valid hash (proof of work)
The block's own "fingerprint", calculated from **all** of the contents above

blocks.content:
┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐
   │ Block 0 (genesis)   │    │ Block 1             │    │ Block 2             │
   │ Data: first record  │    │ Data: A → B 10      │    │ Data: B → C 4       │
   │ Prev hash: 0000     │ ┌─►│ Prev hash: 1A2F     │ ┌─►│ Prev hash: 7C9E     │
   │ Nonce: 3108         │ │  │ Nonce: 9921         │ │  │ Nonce: 0457         │
   │ Hash: 1A2F ─────────┼─┘  │ Hash: 7C9E ─────────┼─┘  │ Hash: 44B0          │
   └─────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘
   Each block stores the hash of the previous block, so the blocks form a chain.
blocks.caption: Blocks linked by hashes

blocks.content: The **first** block of a blockchain. It has no block before it, so its "previous hash" is a fixed value such as all zeros.

A function that converts data of **any length** into a **fixed-length** string of characters (the **hash** or digest). Blockchains such as Bitcoin use **SHA-256**, which always gives 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters).

items.title: Properties of a cryptographic hash
items.content:
- **Fixed length** — a word and a whole book both give a 64-character SHA-256 hash.
- **Deterministic** — the same data always gives the **same** hash.
- **One-way** — the original data **cannot be worked out** from the hash.
- **Avalanche effect** — a tiny change in the data gives a **completely different** hash.
- **Collision-resistant** — it is practically impossible to find two different inputs with the same hash.

blocks.title: The avalanche effect (real SHA-256 hashes)
blocks.content:
| Data | SHA-256 hash |
|---|---|
| `Aida pays Bek 10` | `58fac423c8099c22…1e726b74` |
| `Aida pays Bek 90` | `b5ac3f0990250b67…4086512a` |

Changing **one digit** of the amount produces a totally different hash — so any change to a block is **detected immediately**.

items.title: Public and private keys
items.content:
- Every user has a **key pair**.
- The **private key** is kept **secret** — it is used to **sign** transactions.
- The **public key** (and the **address** made from it) is shared — others use it to send coins and to **check** signatures.

items.title: Digital signature
items.content:
- The sender signs the transaction with their **private key**.
- Any node can **verify** the signature with the sender's **public key**.
- This proves the transaction really comes from the owner and has **not been changed**.

items.title: Wallet
items.content:
- Software or a device that stores a user's **keys** and shows their balance.
- Coins are not "inside" the wallet — the blockchain records them; the wallet holds the keys that control them.
- **Lost private key = lost coins**: there is no bank to reset it.

blocks.title: Adding a transaction to the blockchain
items: A user **requests** a transaction (e.g. send 1 coin to Asel) and **signs** it with their **private key**.
The transaction is **broadcast** to the peer-to-peer network of nodes.
Nodes **validate** it — they check the digital signature and that the sender has enough balance (no double spending).
Valid transactions are grouped together into a new **block**.
Nodes reach **consensus** — e.g. a miner solves the **proof-of-work** puzzle.
The new block, containing the hash of the previous block, is **added to the chain** and **copied to every node**.
The transaction is **complete** and permanent.

blocks.content:
User signs        Broadcast to         Nodes          Grouped        Consensus       Block added
   transaction  ──►  the network    ──►  validate   ──►  into a    ──►  (mining /  ──►  to every
   (private key)     of nodes            signature      new block       proof of        copy of
                                         + balance                      work)           the chain
blocks.caption: The process

blocks.content: The set of rules by which the nodes of a decentralised network **agree** which new block is valid and gets added, without a central authority.

blocks.title: Proof of work and proof of stake
rows: **Miners** compete to solve a hard mathematical puzzle
**Validators** chosen according to the coins they **stake** (lock up)
Change the **nonce** again and again until the block's hash starts with a required number of zeros
Selected validator proposes the block; others check it
**Very high** — millions of hash calculations per second
The cost of electricity and hardware

blocks.content: The process in proof of work where nodes (**miners**) repeatedly change the **nonce** and calculate the block's hash until it meets the **difficulty target** (e.g. starts with "0000"). The first miner to succeed broadcasts the block and receives a **reward**. Finding the hash is hard, but **checking** it is easy for the other nodes.

blocks.title: What happens if someone changes an old block
items: An attacker changes the amount in **Block 1** from 10 to 90.
Block 1's **hash changes** completely (avalanche effect).
**Block 2** still stores the **old** hash as its "previous hash", so the **link is broken**.
To hide the change, the attacker would have to **re-mine Block 1, Block 2 and every later block** — each needing proof of work.
Meanwhile the honest network keeps adding new blocks, and the attacker's copy also differs from the copies on **all the other nodes**.
Nodes accept the version held by the **majority**, so the altered chain is **rejected**.

blocks.title: The 51 % attack
blocks.content: If one person or group controlled **more than half** of the network's computing power (or stake), they could out-pace the honest nodes and rewrite recent blocks. On large networks such as Bitcoin this would be **extremely expensive**, which is why big public blockchains are considered secure.

blocks.title: Types of blockchain
rows: **Anyone** can read, send transactions and become a node
Banks sharing settlement records; supply-chain partners

blocks.content: A **program stored on the blockchain** that **runs automatically** when agreed conditions are met, without a middle-man. Example: when a delivery is confirmed, the payment is released to the supplier automatically.

blocks.title: Uses of blockchain technology
rows: Payments between people **without a bank**; no double spending
Insurance paid automatically when a flight is delayed
Faster and cheaper than through several banks
Tracking food or medicines from producer to shop
Every step recorded; fakes are detected
Employers can verify them; cannot be forged
Ownership records cannot be secretly changed
Proof of who owns a digital item

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
rows: Very hard to tamper with — **high data integrity**
**Proof of work** uses huge amounts of **electricity**
**No central authority** and no single point of failure
**Slow** — limited number of transactions per second
Mistakes **cannot be undone**; **lost private keys** mean lost assets
Fewer **intermediaries** → lower fees, faster international payments
Every node stores the whole chain → **large storage** needs
Records are **permanent** with timestamps — a full audit trail
**Legal and regulatory** uncertainty; cryptocurrencies used in some crimes
Data on a public chain is **visible** to everyone (privacy)

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe what blockchain technology is. [1]**
A **distributed database** shared among the **nodes** of a computer network / a growing list of records (**blocks**) **linked using cryptography** / a technology for keeping a **secure, decentralised** record of transactions (1).

**Q: Give one example of using blockchain technology. [1]**
Cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin) / smart contracts / financial services / games / supply chain / domain names (1).

**Q: Explain how a blockchain prevents a record from being changed. [3]**
Each block contains the **hash of the previous block** (1); changing data changes that block's **hash**, so it no longer matches the next block and the chain is broken (1); every node has a **copy**, so the altered chain differs from the majority and is **rejected** (1).

**Q: Describe the role of miners. [2]**
Miners **validate** transactions and group them into a block (1); they compete to solve the **proof-of-work** puzzle (find a nonce giving a valid hash) and the winner adds the block and is **rewarded** (1).

- Saying blockchain is "stored on one secure server" — it is **distributed** across many nodes.
- Saying a hash can be **decrypted** — hashing is **one-way**, it is not encryption.
- Confusing the **private** key (secret, used to sign) with the **public** key (shared, used to verify).
- Writing "blockchain = Bitcoin" — Bitcoin is just **one use** of blockchain.
- Forgetting that each block stores the **previous** block's hash — this is what forms the chain.
